chunks: Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurara, who said:

Abdullah ibn Umeyr al-Laythi came to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'What do you say regarding the Mut'ah of women?' He said, 'Allah permitted it in His Book and upon the tongue of His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), so it is permissible until the Day of Resurrection.'
He said, 'O Abu Ja'far! The likes of you say this, and yet Umar prohibited it and forbade it.' He said, 'Even if he did so.'
He said, 'I seek refuge with Allah for you from that, that you should permit something which Umar has prohibited.'

So he said to him, 'So you are upon the saying of your companion, and I am upon the saying of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). So come, I shall curse you if the true saying is what the Messenger of Allah said, and the falsehood is what your companion said.'
He said, so Abdullah ibn Umeyr turned to him and said, 'Would it please you if your wives, and your daughters, and your sisters, and the daughters of your paternal uncle did it?'
So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) turned away from him when he mentioned his wives and the daughters of his paternal uncle.
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on Mut'ah and how does it differ from the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'al-Imam al-Sadiq's' assertion of the permanence of Mut'ah by contrasting divine revelation with the subsequent practice of Umar ibn al-Khattab. The Imam challenges Abdullah ibn Umeyr to a mutual cursing (li'an) to prove that the Prophet's permission supersedes Umar's prohibition, emphasizing that the validity of the ruling rests on the Quran and Sunnah rather than companion consensus. This narrative serves as a foundational argument for Shia scholars against the Sunni view that Umar's abrogation or prohibition was binding.
